passages.happening:
“This is a trustworthy saying: If anyone aspires to be an overseer, he desires a noble task” (verse 1).

“An overseer, then, must be above reproach, the husband of but one wife, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not dependent on wine, not violent but gentle, peaceable, and free of the love of money” (verses 2-3). He must manage his own household well, “For if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how can he care for the church of God?” (verse 5). He must not be a recent convert, or he may become proud, and he must have a good reputation with outsiders (verses 6-7).
passages.hearers:
‘Overseer’ means one who watches over. Older English Bibles say ‘bishop’, and the word later came to mean that. But in the New Testament it names a local church leader, and it seems to be another name for an elder. Paul called the elders of Ephesus together and told them the Holy Spirit had made them overseers (Acts 20:17, 28).

Look at the list. Almost every item is about character, not talent. Most of it is what any decent person in that world would admire: self-control, temperance, hospitality, no drunkenness, no violence. Paul's point is not that leaders need rare virtues. It is that they must really have the ordinary ones, so that no one outside the church can point at them and laugh. Only two items are special to the church: the overseer must be ‘able to teach’, and must not be a new believer.

‘Hospitable’ mattered. Inns were few and often rough, and travelling believers depended on the homes of church members. The church itself met in homes. An overseer's door had to be open.

The household was the basic unit of that world: the family, its dependents, and often its slaves. How a man ran it was a public test of his character. So Paul reasons from the smaller to the larger. If you cannot care for your own home, you cannot care for God's.

And notice what is missing. Nothing about being impressive, wealthy, a great speaker or a natural leader. The one thing the false teachers in Ephesus had, confident talk, is not on the list.
passages.ot:
Moses was told to choose leaders by their character: “select capable men from among the people—God-fearing, trustworthy men who are averse to dishonest gain” (Exodus 18:21). Israel was to choose “wise, understanding, and respected men” (Deuteronomy 1:13).

The prophets condemned leaders who served themselves. “Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves! Should not the shepherds feed their flock?” (Ezekiel 34:2). Micah grieved that “her priests teach for a price” (Micah 3:11).

And the danger of a new leader's pride is old wisdom: “Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18).
passages.hard:
Must church leaders today meet this list, and how do churches differ?

Churches are ordered in different ways, and each reads these verses in its own light. Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches, and Methodist churches in their own form, are led by bishops who oversee many congregations. Presbyterian and Reformed churches are led by elders who govern together. Baptist, Congregational and many free churches hold that each local congregation, under Christ, chooses its own leaders. These notes do not choose.

Christians read ‘the husband of but one wife’ in several ways: a man faithful in marriage (the Greek says, literally, ‘a one-woman man’), a ban on having more than one wife, a ban on remarriage after divorce, or a rule that leaders must be married. Churches also differ on whether the office of overseer is open to women. Complementarian Christians note that the qualities are stated in male terms and that the chapter follows directly on 2:12. Egalitarian Christians note that verse 1 opens with ‘If anyone’ and read the phrase about one wife as aimed at faithfulness rather than at excluding women, much as the same phrase is used of widows in 5:9. These notes do not choose.

What every reading shares is that character comes before gifting. A gifted leader who is violent, greedy, harsh, proud or deceitful does not meet Paul's standard, however well he preaches or however much his church grows.

And nothing in this passage shields a leader who does harm. Christians agree that leaders are servants accountable to Christ and to his word, and that no authority may be used to cover abuse. If a leader uses his place to control, exploit or harm, these verses do not protect him. Anyone harmed by a church leader is free to speak to another trusted leader, a counselor, or, where a crime is involved, the authorities. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul's list asks more about who a leader is than what a leader can do. Ask what you look for in a leader: gifts and results, or character. Ask which of these qualities you would most need to grow in, whether or not you lead. And ask whether your home is a place where the care you show matches the faith you profess.

passages.happening:
“Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued or given to much wine or greedy for money. They must hold to the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience. Additionally, they must first be tested. Then, if they are above reproach, let them serve as deacons” (verses 8-10).

“In the same way, the women must be dignified, not slanderers, but temperate and faithful in all things” (verse 11).

“A deacon must be the husband of but one wife, a good manager of his children and of his own household. For those who have served well as deacons acquire for themselves a high standing and great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus” (verses 12-13).
passages.hearers:
‘Deacon’ means servant. It was the ordinary word for someone who waits on others or carries out a task. Jesus used it of himself: he came ‘not to be served, but to serve’ (Mark 10:45). Here it has become the name of a recognized group in the church, though Paul says little about what deacons did. Acts tells of seven men chosen to care for widows so that the apostles could keep praying and preaching (Acts 6:1-6), and many see the beginning of deacons there.

Once again the list is about character. ‘Not double-tongued’ means not saying one thing to one person and another to the next. In a church that met in homes, a servant who carried tales from one house to another could do great harm. ‘Not greedy for money’ mattered because deacons may have handled the church's gifts to the poor.

‘They must first be tested.’ A church should watch a person's life over time before giving them a task. That protects the church, and it protects the person.

Then verse 11 speaks of ‘the women’, right in the middle of the part about deacons. Who are they? Christians read it two ways, as the part below sets out.

And the reward of serving well is not money or power. It is ‘a high standing’ and ‘great confidence in the faith’. Those who serve quietly grow bold in Christ.
passages.ot:
God's people have always needed trusted servants to help bear the load. When Moses was worn out, God told him to gather seventy elders: “They will help you bear the burden of the people, so that you do not have to bear it by yourself” (Numbers 11:17).

The Psalms ask for faithful servants and refuse deceitful ones: “he who walks in the way of integrity shall minister to me. No one who practices deceit shall dwell in my house” (Psalm 101:6-7). And Proverbs warns about the double tongue Paul names: “A gossip reveals a secret, but a trustworthy person keeps a confidence” (Proverbs 11:13).
passages.hard:
In verse 11, who are ‘the women’: deacons' wives, or women who were deacons?

Christians read it both ways, and these notes do not choose.

Some read them as the wives of deacons. They note that verse 11 sits between two parts about male deacons, and that verse 12 goes straight back to deacons as husbands. On this reading Paul asks that a deacon's wife share his good character, since she would often share his work.

Others read them as women who were deacons. They note that the same Greek word, ‘likewise’ or ‘in the same way’, introduces a new group in verse 8 and again in verse 11; that the Greek has no word for ‘their’, so it does not say ‘their wives’; that Paul calls Phoebe a deacon of the church in Cenchrea, using the same word (Romans 16:1); and that around AD 112 a Roman governor, Pliny, wrote of two slave women whom the Christians called ministers.

Churches today follow both readings. Some have women deacons and some do not, and both read this verse with care.
passages.asks: Deacons are servants, chosen for character and tested over time. Ask where you are serving, and whether anyone could test your faithfulness by watching your life. Ask whether your words are the same to every person, or whether you are double-tongued. And ask whether you think of serving as a lower calling, or as the way of Christ.

passages.t: God's household, and the mystery of godliness
passages.happening:
“Although I hope to come to you soon, I am writing you these things in case I am delayed, so that you will know how each one must conduct himself in God’s household, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth” (verses 14-15).

“By common confession, the mystery of godliness is great: He appeared in the flesh, was vindicated by the Spirit, was seen by angels, was proclaimed among the nations, was believed in throughout the world, was taken up in glory” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
These verses are the hinge of the letter. Paul says why he is writing: so that the church will know how to live as ‘God's household’. Not a club, not a lecture hall, but a family, the household of ‘the living God’.

Then he calls the church ‘the pillar and foundation of the truth’. Ephesus was famous for the great columns of its temple of Artemis. Paul says the church is a different kind of pillar. It holds up the truth and shows it to the world.

And what is the truth? Paul answers with what seems to be an early Christian song or confession. ‘By common confession’ means it is what all believers say together. It has six short lines that move back and forth between earth and heaven:

He appeared in the flesh. Christ came as a real human being.
He was vindicated by the Spirit. The Spirit showed him to be in the right; many read this of his resurrection.
He was seen by angels.
He was proclaimed among the nations.
He was believed in throughout the world.
He was taken up in glory.

‘Mystery’ in Paul does not mean a puzzle. It means something once hidden in God's plan and now made known. The great mystery of godliness is not a rule. It is a person, and his story.
passages.ot:
God dwelling among his people is the hope of the Old Testament. When the tabernacle was finished, “the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle” (Exodus 40:34). Solomon wondered, “But will God indeed dwell upon the earth?” (1 Kings 8:27). In Christ, who ‘appeared in the flesh’, he did.

The nations hearing and believing is the promise of the prophets and Psalms: “All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the LORD” (Psalm 22:27). “The LORD has bared His holy arm in the sight of all the nations” (Isaiah 52:10).

And the angels who see him are the ones Isaiah heard crying, “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts; all the earth is full of His glory” (Isaiah 6:3).
passages.asks: Paul says the church is God's household and the pillar of the truth, and that the truth is Christ. Ask whether your church feels like a household or a club. Ask whether the way you live holds up the truth about Christ or hides it. And ask which line of the song you most need to hear today.
